newsitem.title: USA: China refuses to renounce force against Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China refuses to renounce force against Taiwan.

text.p: In a blunt speech to U.S. military officers, Chinese Defense Minister Chi Haotian said on Tuesday that China refuses to renounce the use of force to reclaim Taiwan, which Beijing considers a rogue province.

"We hope to see a peaceful settlement, yet we refuse to renounce the use of force," the visiting minister told officers at the military's National Defense University. He said the Beijing government would "not sit idly by" and allow Taiwan leaders continue "conniving" to split China.
Chi's statement was not new, but his comments on a visit to improve U.S.-China relations emphasized the importance that Communist China gives to reclaiming democratic Taiwan.

The United States, under the 1972 Shanghai Communique, recognizes Beijing as the sole government of China, but maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan and continues to sell arms to the island located off China.

Chi urged Washington, which earlier this year dispatched two aircraft carriers to the region and accused China of trying to influence Taiwan's presidential elections with a show of military force in the Taiwan Strait, to let Beijing and Taipei settle their differences without interference.

"The Taiwan authorities have, in disregard of the overall interests of the Chinese nation, gone farther and farther down the road of conniving at, and participating in, activities aimed at splitting the motherland, which cause tensions in cross-strait relations," Chi said.

"I would like to point out here that if those elements on (the) island, who are eager to see China dismembered and themselves become more important with foreign support, should cling to their wrong cause and slip further astray, the Chinese government and people will not sit idly by."
Chi is beginning a two-week visit to the United States, which was postponed earlier this year because of U.S.-China tensions over Taiwan.
He held talks with President Bill Clinton and Defense Secretary William Perry on Monday.
Talks with Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott later on Tuesday were described as "positive, frank and constructive."

A State Department spokesman said Chi and Talbott discussed a wide range of issues including non-proliferation, the value of military-to-military contacts, the situation on the Korean Peninsula, global arms control and trade.
Chi raised Chinese concerns about Taiwan and U.S. arms sales in particular, he said. Talbott also discussed Washington's concerns about human rights during the meeting.

Despite differences on Taiwan, trade and Chinese arms sales to Pakistan and Iran, the United States and China are moving to improve relations based on areas of mutual interest such as a desire for peace in Korea and economic stability in the western Pacific.

Chi's visit has prompted strong objections from Republican members of Congress, who noted that he was China's top military officer when the People's Liberation Army crushed a 1989 revolt in Tiananmen Square, reportedly killing hundreds of Chinese civilians.
Chi said in a response to a question from one American officer on Tuesday that the incident had been exaggerated by reporters, but said troops had to use force in response to some protestors.
"Our bilateral relations have zig-zagged in recent years," Chi told the mid-level U.S. military officers, many who will someday become generals and admirals in the U.S. armed forces.

But he said precedent had shown that if the two countries work with each other on an equal footing and with mutual respect, "we will be able to gradually iron out the specific problems in our bilateral relations."
